query: Earlier automotive-catalyst research reported that Cu–Ni catalysts can oxidize CO and hydrocarbons at lower temperatures without platinum-group metals, while Pd–Cu and Pt–Cu catalysts can resist poisoning by H2O and NO and enable oxidation below 150 °C. Multi-principal-element catalysts in nearly equiatomic ratios have also been explored as a framework for combining high activity, thermal stability, and reduced platinum-group-metal use. These prior results demonstrate individual capabilities but do not establish the combined performance demanded by increasingly stringent regulations: clean exhaust during transient and low-temperature operation, resistance to relevant poisons, and durability over a vehicle lifetime despite the mileage-related degradation observed in real-driving-emission studies. Starting from a near-equiatomic, multi-principal-element automotive alloy catalyst, what single intervention could address this combined activity, poisoning-resistance, and lifetime-durability problem without sacrificing low platinum-group-metal use? State one hypothesis identifying the intervention, explaining how it would work, predicting the change relative to the unmodified catalyst, defining the exhaust and aging conditions over which it should apply, citing supporting prior evidence, and specifying an experiment whose result would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: An ultrathin, in situ formed CeO2 overlayer on the near‐equiatomic multi‐principal‐element alloy catalyst will simultaneously enhance its low-temperature oxidation activity, resistance to H2O/NO poisoning, and long-term durability without increasing platinum-group-metal content.
generation.material_initial_state: A near-equiatomic, multi-principal-element automotive alloy catalyst with low platinum-group-metal use and a predominantly metallic surface.
generation.intervention: Introduce a controlled oxidation step to form an ultrathin, well-dispersed CeO2 overlayer on the catalyst surface.
generation.conditions: Catalyst operation under simulated automotive exhaust conditions—transient, low-temperature operation (<150 °C) with the presence of typical poisons such as water vapor and NO, followed by accelerated aging protocols representative of vehicle lifetime.
generation.structural_mediator: The CeO2 overlayer that couples with the alloy surface, creating a metal/oxide interface with abundant oxygen vacancies.
generation.mechanism: CeO2 is known to provide oxygen storage capacity and facilitate redox cycling. The overlayer can supply active oxygen species to promote oxidation of CO and hydrocarbons at lower temperatures, while its oxygen mobility helps remove poisoning species (e.g., adsorbed H2O/NO) and physically stabilize the alloy surface against sintering over long-term operation.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the unmodified alloy, the CeO2-modified catalyst will demonstrate lower light-off temperatures for CO/hydrocarbon oxidation, enhanced resistance to deactivation from H2O and NO exposure, and improved durability (smaller performance drop over induced aging cycles).
generation.baseline: The performance metrics (light-off temperature, poison-resistance, and durability) of the unmodified multi-principal-element alloy catalyst under identical exhaust conditions.
generation.boundary: The improvement is expected only if the CeO2 overlayer is sufficiently thin and well-integrated with the alloy surface; an excessively thick oxide or poor interface formation may instead reduce active site accessibility and overall performance.
generation.uncertainty: The optimal thickness and formation conditions of the CeO2 layer remain to be determined. It is also uncertain how the overlayer's structural integrity will be maintained under realistic cyclic redox conditions over an extended vehicle lifetime.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two catalyst sets: (1) the baseline near-equiatomic multi-principal-element alloy catalyst and (2) an identical catalyst subjected to a controlled in situ oxidation treatment to form an ultrathin CeO2 overlayer. Expose both sets to simulated automotive exhaust conditions at low temperatures (<150 °C) with controlled amounts of H2O and NO. Then, subject the catalysts to accelerated aging processes mimicking extended vehicle operation.
measurements: Light-off temperatures for CO and hydrocarbon oxidation
Conversion efficiencies under poisoning conditions (H2O/NO presence)
Durability metrics (activity retention after aging cycles)
Surface characterizations (TEM, XPS to verify CeO2 layer quality and thickness)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the CeO2-modified catalyst does not show a statistically significant reduction in light-off temperature, improved tolerance to poisoning and enhanced durability compared to the unmodified catalyst, the hypothesis will be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: A widely used catalyst, Pd/γ-Al2O3, offers high surface area but has some disadvantages such as high cost and low thermal stability [,,]. It is known that the PdO/Al2O3 catalyst is not stable at high temperatures due to PdO reduction and surface area loss, which necessitates the exploration of mixed oxide catalysts [,]. La2O3 is commonly added to enhance PdO stability and preserve γ-Al2O3’s surface area, improving the catalyst’s durability []. Complex catalysts are synthesized by the co-impregnation of Pd and La salts, often with a third element, to obtain a three-element system on γ-Al2O3 or ceramic supports. These mixed catalysts enhanced methane oxidation at high temperatures. The addition of La2O3 and BaO stabilizes the alumina surface, while CeO2 and NiO prevent PdO reduction []. On the other hand, ceria enhances oxygen storage by increasing surface oxygen mobility, and La2O3 addition reduces the CeO2 particle size, prevents sintering, and improves reducibility. In general, Ce-La-based compounds offer good catalytic activity due to their oxygen storage and surface basicity []. cited_evidence.kind: web:Unraveling the Alkaline HER Mechanism on HEA Surfaces
cited_evidence.text: To elucidate how elemental composition influences the HER pathway, we systematically evaluated the adsorption behavior of H2O and *OH species across various active sites in the FeCoNiCuM HEA models (Figure B,C, Tables S8 and S9). Adsorption energies (E ads) were averaged over three representative top sites for each element to ensure robustness and statistical reliability. Stronger adsorption of H2O and *OH typically facilitates faster water dissociation by enhancing electron transfer and stabilizing key intermediates. , As expected, oxophilic dopants such as Ti, Zr, V, Nb, Mo, and W exhibit significantly more negative E ads values, indicative of strong interactions with oxygen-containing species. In contrast, base metal sites show a gradation of adsorption strength, with Fe exhibiting moderately strong binding, followed by Co and Ni, while Cu sites display the weakest, or even slightly positive, adsorption energies. This suggests that Fe plays a primary role in anchoring intermediates during the Volmer step, whereas Cu may promote efficient desorption and prevent surface poisoning, thereby complementing the overall reaction kinetics.
